role: effect modifier (confounder only in single-place before/after)
bias_path: Common to treated and controls, so a comparison design removes the level shift. But high rates shrink the policy effect itself: fewer projects pencil and owner-builders can't borrow. A before/after design reads a rate slump as policy failure (Portland RIP ran into 3%->7% in 2021-23).
design_response: Never rely on own pre-period alone; year effects in DiD/SC remove the common shock. Estimate effect x rate-regime interaction where comparables span different rate periods (Portland 2010 low, CA 2017-23 across the shock).
model_response: Enters feasibility (financing cost in pro forma) and the uptake hazard; user slider with today's rate as default.
data_sources: FRED MORTGAGE30US (Freddie Mac PMMS); FRED prime rate

bias_path: Common shock (lumber 2021). Shifts how many parcels pencil, so the same reform yields less when costs spike.
design_response: Year effects remove the common level; deflate all dollars with PPI.
model_response: Pro forma hard-cost input; slider (sponsor named construction cost as the example sensitivity).
data_sources: BLS PPI inputs to residential construction; RSMeans as parameter source only (proprietary)

factor: National demand shocks (COVID, remote work, 2022 rate spike)
role: confounder for single-place designs; timing threat
bias_path: Lands in the post-period of 2019-21 reforms (Minneapolis 2020, LA Dec-2019 ordinance). Remote work moved demand toward suburbs and backyard space, which could inflate ADU uptake independent of the rules.
design_response: Year effects; population-growth placebo SC (as Lower Hutt did); sensitivity run dropping 2020-21.
model_response: Baseline forecast scenario, not part of the policy effect.
data_sources: Census population estimates; IRS SOI migration

factor: Local labor demand, migration, income growth
bias_path: Booming places both reform and build more. Not removed by year effects because it differs by place.
design_response: Match/SC on the pre-reform outcome path; add a shift-share (Bartik) employment index built from pre-period industry mix, which the reform can't affect. Use pre-period covariates only.
model_response: Drives the baseline forecast per jurisdiction.
data_sources: BLS QCEW county employment; Census population estimates; ACS income

factor: Pre-reform prices and rents (housing pressure) driving adoption
role: confounder via selection into treatment (largest threat)
bias_path: Cities reform because prices are surging, and surging prices raise construction on their own. Stacy et al.'s falsification test found rents already moving before loosening reforms.
design_response: SC/matching on pre-reform price level and path; event-study leads; HonestDiD bounds; placebo dates.
model_response: Same variable re-used as the price-to-cost regime modifier (C40) and as a transport covariate.
data_sources: FHFA HPI (county/metro); Zillow ZHVI/ZORI (terms); ACS median rent

bias_path: Some places were already on a rising path (Austin ADUs; reformers in Stacy et al. had rising unit counts pre-reform), so a post-reform level looks like an effect.
design_response: Match on demeaned pre-period outcomes (Ferman-Pinto SC as in Auckland/Lower Hutt); flat event-study leads required.
model_response: Baseline forecast carries the trend; policy effect is measured against it.

bias_path: The same council that legalises ADUs also speeds permits, waives fees, publishes pre-approved plans. Effect of 'the law' absorbs the whole package.
design_response: Code the full reform bundle (C08); within-city eligible-vs-ineligible contrasts cancel citywide political climate; report as package effect where it can't be separated.
model_response: Local levers shown as separate optional toggles, not folded into the benchmark effect.

bias_path: Portland 2010 SDC waiver coincided with a size-limit increase; Lower Hutt had a fee waiver and parking changes; NYC rezonings were bundled with infrastructure; Seattle 2019 ADU reform coincided with MHA upzoning; SB 9 overlaps CA ADU laws.
design_response: Reform-vector coding with dates for every component; treat as bundle when simultaneous; exploit staggered timing to separate where possible.
model_response: Combined-scenario engine uses one parcel allocation so stacked reforms don't double count.

bias_path: Iterative reforms get credited to the first one, the same ordinance appears at several legislative stages, and late reforms are coded with post-periods they couldn't have affected. Mis-dating pulls estimates toward zero or shifts the ramp.
design_response: Each amendment is a dose increment with its own date; event time starts at the first period the outcome could react (Abadie); anticipation window tested.
model_response: Ramp curve indexed to the effective date of the full-strength rule.

factor: Reform design strictness (owner-occupancy, size/FAR caps, parking, min lot, by-right vs discretionary)
bias_path: Coding a weak law the same as a strong one averages the effect toward zero. Minneapolis (FAR binding) produced ~1% of units in 2-4 plexes; Portland and Spokane far more. Density limits, not use permission, bind (Boston RD).
design_response: Constraint score from the coding rubric; estimate dose-response; use weak-reform places as contrast, not as controls.
model_response: Benchmark scenarios fix design to the Handbook; local toggles show design effects.

factor: Local implementation and opt-out of state laws
role: treatment measurement (de jure vs de facto)
bias_path: A state mandate can be neutralised locally: 68% of Connecticut towns opted out of PA 21-29; pre-2017 California cities wrote ordinances that blunted state ADU law; SB 9 projects hit lien-release rules, $30-50k lot-split fees and $50-100k utility connection fees.
design_response: Code effective treatment per jurisdiction; report intent-to-treat (state law) and effective-treatment estimates separately.
model_response: State-law scenario multiplies by an 'effective adoption' share; user can set it.
data_sources: Local ordinances; state compliance reports (e.g. CA HCD); DesegregateCT

bias_path: Deed restrictions block ADUs and plexes regardless of zoning, so eligible-parcel counts overstate the real pool. HOA-dense areas show lower uptake in California.
design_response: Flag or exclude HOA parcels where identifiable; test uptake by subdivision age as proxy.
model_response: Eligibility haircut parameter by area; data-tier flag where HOA data is missing.
data_sources: State HOA registries where they exist; subdivision plat year from assessor (proxy)

bias_path: A reform only matters where the old limit was below what the market wanted. Zurich effects appear only where zoning bound; NYC effects scale with capacity increase; Houston townhouses went mostly to non-SF land.
design_response: Dose = change in allowed capacity vs built/market-desired density; split bound vs non-bound areas.
model_response: Feasibility test per parcel only counts parcels where the new rule beats the old use.
data_sources: Assessor building sq ft and units vs zoning limits

factor: Parcel stock: lot size, existing-structure value, house age/size, garage/alley
bias_path: Cost of tearing down or building around the existing house drives uptake. Redevelopment premium depends on improvement-to-land value; ADUs less likely on large lots with newer homes in LA; teardowns favour small old homes.
design_response: Use as matching/transport covariates; stratify hazard by these where parcel data exist.
model_response: Parcel-level hazard multipliers (tier 1); distributions estimated for tier 2-3 places.
data_sources: Assessor rolls / state parcel layers (lot area, improvement and land value, year built)

bias_path: ADUs are mostly built by resident owners; multigenerational households add demand. Uptake differs by tenure and household type (more common in Latino areas of LA).
design_response: Transport covariate; split eligibility by owner vs renter occupied where possible.
model_response: Hazard multiplier by tenure share.
data_sources: ACS tenure and household type; assessor homestead flags

factor: Location and access (jobs, transit, commercial districts)
bias_path: Uptake clusters near jobs, commercial districts and transit; bus access gained importance after LA's reform.
design_response: Covariate in parcel models; not needed for city-level DiD.
model_response: Optional hazard multiplier in tier-1 parcel mode.

bias_path: Upzoning raises land prices (Auckland, Minneapolis, Chicago) or lowers them (Houston); fee cuts partly flow into land. Controlling for post-reform land or house prices removes part of the real effect.
design_response: Use pre-period values only; never put post-reform prices on the right-hand side.
model_response: Modelled as a feedback inside the pro forma (land-capture share), with a slider.

factor: Fee incidence (share of a fee cut captured by landowners)
bias_path: Where price sits well above production cost, a fee cut becomes land value, not homes. Pass-through ~$1.60 per $1 in Dade; 75% absorbed in a weak Contra Costa submarket.
design_response: Use incidence studies to bound lambda by market regime.
model_response: lambda_land parameter (0.25-0.75) in fee module; low case includes zero effect.

factor: What fees pay for (water/sewer vs other)
role: effect modifier and confounder for fees
bias_path: Fees fund infrastructure and can buy faster approvals; non-water/sewer fees raised some construction in Florida while water/sewer fees reduced it. Cutting fees without replacing revenue can cut capacity.
design_response: Split fee types; do not treat all fee dollars as pure cost.
model_response: Revenue-replaced vs not-replaced toggle.
data_sources: Local fee schedules; utility fee schedules

bias_path: A sewer moratorium or costly utility upgrade stops building whatever zoning says, and can coincide with reform timing.
design_response: Code moratoria as shocks; exclude affected place-years or add indicator.
model_response: Eligibility exclusion where capacity is known to bind.
data_sources: Utility district notices; state environmental agencies

factor: Approval time, process and pre-approved plans
bias_path: Delay matters more than fees in the metro panel (1-SD longer delay -> 20-25% fewer permits). Pre-approval raises 4-yr completion 8-12 pp in LA. Seattle ADU approvals ~80 vs ~133 days.
design_response: Measure median days application->issue before and after; code process changes as separate reform components.
model_response: Permit-time slider as a local lever; shifts hazard and carrying cost.
data_sources: Local permit data with application and issue dates

role: effect modifier (the channel through which rates hit ADUs)
bias_path: ADUs are financed by owners, not developers: Portland 62% cash, 2% construction loans; financing is the top barrier in California. Rates and home equity therefore matter differently for ADUs than for plexes.
design_response: Covariate for transport (home equity proxy); interaction with rate regime.
model_response: ADU hazard depends on home equity and rate; separate from developer pro forma used for MM.
data_sources: HMDA home-improvement and HELOC originations by tract; FHFA HPI x tenure

bias_path: Higher price volatility delays development (1-SD more uncertainty -> 11% lower development likelihood in Seattle). Timing cycles make 'feasible' differ from 'built'. A temporary fee cut pulls projects forward.
design_response: Report effects by volatility tercile where sample allows.
model_response: Ramp and hazard parameters; fee module distinguishes permanent vs temporary cut.

factor: Builder capacity, learning and local diffusion
role: effect modifier (ramp shape); source of substitution
bias_path: Uptake keeps rising for years as specialist builders, lenders and designs appear (Portland rose ~6 years); small builders shifting to ADUs can reduce other small-scale building.
design_response: Event-time curves rather than a single post dummy; count distinct contractors in permit data.
model_response: Logistic ramp to steady state; ramp speed is a parameter.
data_sources: Contractor names in local permit data

bias_path: Where greenfield land is abundant, infill reforms compete with easy suburban building. Auckland spillovers tied to undeveloped land in control areas; most Houston townhouses went on non-SF land.
design_response: Covariate in donor choice; displacement analysis by land availability.
model_response: Displacement share higher where greenfield is plentiful.

bias_path: Reform pulls projects from neighbours, inflating the local effect and depressing controls (double counting). Lower Hutt's regional net was +10-18% vs a much larger local effect.
design_response: Drop neighbours from donor pools; run SCs on neighbours; Auckland-style bounds.
model_response: Displacement share parameter (0-50%); show 'in this city' vs 'net statewide'.

bias_path: Controls are covered by the same state law (California ADU law is statewide), reform later (a third of Minneapolis Fed donors), or have unrecorded reforms. All bias toward zero.
design_response: Check every donor against the policy inventory; not-yet-treated controls with cut-off dates; out-of-state controls for statewide laws.
model_response: n/a (affects calibration inputs).

factor: Size and type mismatch between reformers and controls
bias_path: Stacy et al.'s reformers averaged ~200k people vs ~20k for controls; fixed effects alone don't make them comparable.
design_response: Size bands for donors (Minneapolis Fed used 150k-2M); balance check SMD <= 0.1.
model_response: Overlap flag when target lies outside comparables.

bias_path: Owners hold projects until the rule passes, then file at once: a dip then a spike that overstates the effect. Land prices move ~2 years before approval; Auckland plan notified 3 years before operative.
design_response: Date treatment at first period the outcome could react; test 1-2 year anticipation window; exclude implementation window from steady-state estimate.
model_response: Ramp curve begins at announcement; steady state measured after year 3.

bias_path: A plex replaces a single-family rebuild; an ADU replaces an addition. Portland single-dwelling zones went from >50% detached houses to <20% of new units, a mix shift that may be partly substitution. Sao Paulo and Auckland found no fall in single-family building.
design_response: Estimate effect on each building type and on total units; negative effect on old types = cannibalisation.
model_response: Net-new share parameter by scenario.
data_sources: Census BPS by size class; local permits incl. alterations

bias_path: Part of any post-reform ADU spike is legalisation: ~78% of San Jose detached ADU construction 2016-20 was unpermitted.
design_response: Separate conversions from new builds; compare against satellite or address counts where possible.
model_response: Formalisation share parameter subtracted from gross ADU permits.

bias_path: ADU tracking often starts because of the reform: California APR parcel data begins 2018, pre-2018 figures cover only the largest cities; places reclassify ADUs from alterations to new units. A larger count can be a new data system, not new homes.
design_response: Use series with consistent definitions across the reform date; validate pre-period against permit text; record data-regime breaks as a coded variable.
model_response: Data-quality flag on calibration points.
data_sources: CA HCD APR; city permit systems; BPS form C-404

factor: Census BPS imputation and non-reporting places
bias_path: Small places are imputed; ADUs appear only if new-structure. Adds noise and undercounts.
design_response: Use annual totals; Fay-Herriot shrinkage for small places; check imputation flags.
model_response: Wider bands for small or imputed places.

bias_path: Permits overstate homes delivered (NZ ~90-95% completion); completions lag 6-24 months.
design_response: State outcome exactly; completion factor reported separately.
model_response: Completion factor 0.85-0.95 parameter.
data_sources: Census Survey of Construction; local CO data

bias_path: Missing middle often replaces a house; gross permits overstate net gain. Portland units per demolition rose 1.68 -> 3.88.
design_response: Subtract demolitions where recorded.
model_response: Net = gross minus demolitions; parameter where data missing.

factor: What the new unit is used for (STR, office, family)
bias_path: Only ~50-80% of ADUs house a separate household long term; ~10% of Seattle ADUs carry STR licences. Local STR rules change the share.
design_response: Report net-new share range; code STR regulation.
model_response: Net-new share 50-80% slider.

bias_path: Tax treatment of the added unit (e.g. California Prop 13 reassesses only the ADU) changes owner returns and complicates value studies.
design_response: Note as a cross-state difference in transport.
model_response: State-specific note; not a slider.

factor: Natural hazards, insurance and disaster rebuilds
bias_path: High fire-hazard and flood zones are excluded or costlier; disaster rebuilds create local permit spikes unrelated to reform.
design_response: Exclude hazard zones from eligibility; code disaster years as shocks.
model_response: Eligibility exclusion layer.
data_sources: FEMA NFHL; state fire hazard maps

bias_path: Places with tougher overall regulation may blunt any single reform.
design_response: Transport covariate; donor similarity.
model_response: Part of similarity score.

bias_path: Where prices sit near cost, reforms and fee cuts tip projects into feasibility; where prices are far above cost, rules bind and fee cuts go to land. Weak markets show null effects (NYC Jerome Ave; Chicago in a weak period); Zurich effects only where rents were high.
design_response: Stratify comparables by regime; primary transport covariate.
model_response: Drives feasibility and fee incidence; shown in the reconciliation panel.

bias_path: Nearby price effects (-3% within 300 m in LA) can drive new restrictions or repeal, cutting long-run uptake.
design_response: Track subsequent tightening in the policy inventory.
model_response: Note as a downside risk to the 5-year range.

bias_path: Reforms passed at a peak look weak; at a trough look strong. Florida fee cuts happened in the 2009-10 bust; Chicago TOD in a weak period.
design_response: Multi-year baselines; avoid anchoring on 2021-22 boom or 2023 slump; year effects.
model_response: Baseline uses multi-year averages, detrended against metro series.

role: effect modifier (cost step by unit count)
bias_path: Duplexes and townhouses up to 3 stories usually fall under the residential code (IRC); attached buildings of 3+ units usually fall under the commercial code (IBC), which adds sprinklers, accessibility and licensed design. The cost step can make 3-6 unit buildings rare even where zoning allows them, so a weak triplex/fourplex response may reflect the code, not the zoning.
design_response: Report effects by building size (2 / 3-4 / 5-6 / townhouse) separately; code any state amendments that let small multifamily use the residential code.
model_response: Pro forma cost step at 3+ units; unit-mix share per project is a parameter.
data_sources: State building-code adoptions; ICC code scope

bias_path: A townhouse that can be sold needs its own lot; plexes need condo law or remain rentals. Where lot splits are slow, discretionary or costly, projects are rental-only or don't happen. SB 9 faced lien releases and $30-50k lot-split fees; Houston's subdivision rules (and the opt-out) shaped where townhouses went.
design_response: Code lot-split and subdivision path as part of the reform vector (by-right? minimum lot after split? fees?).
model_response: Separate for-sale (townhouse) and rental (plex) pro formas; lot-split friction parameter.
data_sources: Subdivision ordinances; local permit data (plat records)

bias_path: Missing middle is built by small developers who rely on construction loans; 5+ unit projects move to commercial lending, and falling cap rates partly offset rising construction costs. Rates hit MM through this channel, not through homeowner equity.
design_response: Interaction of effect with rate regime across comparables.
model_response: Developer pro forma: construction-loan rate, loan-to-cost, cap rate / sale price; separate from the ADU owner channel (C22).
data_sources: FRED rates; Fed Senior Loan Officer Survey (construction lending standards)

bias_path: Most MM replaces an existing house, so it happens only where land value is high relative to the house on it. Teardown rates run ~0.4%/yr in Chicago city and ~1.3%/yr in hot suburbs; redevelopment premiums depend on improvement-to-land value.
design_response: Stratify hazard by improvement-to-land ratio and house age; count demolitions.
model_response: Feasibility = residual land value of new project > existing-use value x (1 + margin).
data_sources: Assessor land and improvement values; demolition permits

factor: ADU vs missing middle competing for the same lot
bias_path: An owner adding an ADU rarely also builds a duplex; SB 9 applications lost out to ADUs. Running the two scenarios separately and adding them double counts lots.
design_response: Estimate combined effects where both reforms apply; check whether MM uptake falls after ADU legalisation.
model_response: One parcel allocation step in combined runs; each parcel takes its most profitable feasible option.

bias_path: Small infill builders need higher margins and have less capacity than production builders; NZ capacity studies use 17-25% hurdles for infill and 28-39% for apartments. The local presence of small builders shapes uptake speed.
design_response: Report ramp shape; count distinct developers in permit data.
model_response: Profit-hurdle parameter by typology; ramp speed.

factor: Floor-area and height limits bundled with unit allowance
bias_path: Allowing 2-6 units without enough floor area or height makes them unbuildable (Minneapolis: FAR bound, ~1% of units in 2-4 plexes). Boston boundary evidence: density plus height matters, use alone does little. The Handbook frees setbacks and coverage and allows 3 stories, but is silent on FAR.
design_response: Code FAR/height alongside unit allowance in the reform vector; dose-response by allowed floor area.
model_response: Benchmark assumes 3 stories with setbacks/coverage non-binding; state the FAR assumption explicitly.

factor: Fee levels set in response to growth (reverse causality)
bias_path: Fast-growing places adopt and raise impact fees because they are growing, so high fees sit next to high construction in raw data. Panels with fee dummies or levels can show null or positive effects for this reason.
design_response: Use fee changes driven by something other than local growth (court rulings, state caps, size thresholds); never estimate from cross-section fee levels.
model_response: Fee effect enters through the pro forma, with literature bounds, not from a fee-level regression.
data_sources: Fee schedules over time; state legal changes

bias_path: Cutting fees cuts the revenue that pays for water, sewer and roads. Without replacement revenue, capacity limits or concurrency rules can stop projects, offsetting the cost saving. Florida non-water/sewer fees increased some construction.
design_response: Distinguish places that replaced revenue from those that didn't; separate fee types.
model_response: Revenue-replaced vs not-replaced toggle; in 'not replaced', a capacity drag parameter.

factor: Fee structure (flat per unit vs scaled by size)
role: effect modifier on unit size and type
bias_path: Flat per-unit fees fall hardest on small units, so they tilt production toward larger homes; scaled fees do the opposite. California exempts ADUs under 750 sq ft from impact fees, which should produce bunching just below 750 sq ft; Washington now requires fees to scale with size.
design_response: Bunching test at fee thresholds; code fee structure per place.
model_response: Fee cut applied per unit at the Handbook's $50k, with a sensitivity for size-scaled fees.

factor: Fee share of total development cost
bias_path: A $25k cut is a different dose for a $150k ADU than for a $600k unit; real fees found in NC, TX and WI are far below the Handbook's $50k, so a $25k cut there exceeds total actual fees.
design_response: Express every fee change as % of total development cost.
model_response: Dose = change in fee / total development cost by typology.

bias_path: Fees paid at permit add financing carry through construction; deferring to final inspection or sale (as Washington requires for single-family) lowers the effective cost without cutting the fee.
design_response: Code payment timing alongside fee level.
model_response: Carry cost of fees in the pro forma depends on payment date.
